equity.at: Common stock: claims, types and risks
equity.say: Alright, this is Module three, equity securities and investment companies. First question: what do you own when you own stock? Common stock is ownership. You share in the company's assets and earnings, and you get a vote, usually by proxy, but nobody promises you a payment. A bondholder is the opposite. A bondholder is a lender: fixed interest, principal back, no ownership, and first claim if the company is liquidated. So the stockholder sits last, holding the residual claim, and because there's no fixed return, stock carries the higher expected return. The quick tell: proportionate share and vote means stock; fixed payment and priority claim means bond. Now the types, and the worked example shows why they matter. Rafael is sixty-one, worried about a recession, and wants one stock that holds up. The automaker and the restaurant chain are cyclical, so their earnings drop in a downturn. The robotics start-up is emerging growth, high risk. The grocery chain sells necessities, which makes it defensive, the best fit. The common mistake is mixing up income stocks, which are about steady dividends, with defensive stocks, which are about resisting the cycle. And know the four risks: market, interest rate, business, and financial, where more debt financing means more financial risk. The exam trap: stockholders never rank ahead of bondholders in liquidation, and the issuer can't deduct dividends the way it deducts interest. With a client, you'd say: when you own stock you own a slice of the business, so you share the upside, but nobody owes you a payment, and we mix cyclical and steady companies so one bad stretch doesn't sink the plan.

Rights and warrants both give you the right to buy the issuer's stock at a set price, but they exist for different reasons, and the exam loves to swap them. Rights protect existing owners. When a company issues new shares, rights let current holders keep their ownership percentage. They're short-lived, just a few weeks, and the exercise price starts below market. Warrants are the sweetener. They're attached to a bond or preferred issue to make it easier to sell, they're long-dated, often five years or more, and the exercise price starts above market. The tell: maintain ownership percentage means rights; sweetener or equity kicker means warrants. Versus a listed call option, a warrant is created by the corporation with customized terms, while a call is written by an individual and standardized by the O C C. Walk the worked example. Lena pays two dollars a share for warrants on eighty shares with a twenty-five dollar exercise price, and the stock climbs to thirty-one. The gain per share is six dollars. Subtract the two dollar warrant cost and she nets four dollars a share. Times eighty shares, that's a three hundred twenty dollar profit, with only one hundred sixty dollars at risk. The wrong answers come from forgetting to subtract the warrant cost, or adding it. The exam trap: warrants are customized, not standardized, and attaching them lets the issuer pay a lower coupon or dividend, which cuts its cost of capital. With a client, you'd say: these rights let you buy new shares at a discount so your ownership isn't watered down, so use them or sell them, but don't let them lapse, because they expire in a few weeks.

equity.at: Cash dividends, dates, DRIPs and taxation
equity.say: Cash dividends. The key idea is that a dividend exists only once the board declares it, unlike bond interest, which is owed. Only shareholders of record on the record date receive it. The date that actually decides things for a buyer is the ex-dividend date. It's the first trading day a buyer does not get the declared dividend, so you have to buy before it. Under T plus one settlement, the book places the record date one business day after the ex-date. Now the payout ratio, which is dividends per share divided by earnings per share. Walk the example. Halvern earns three dollars and twenty cents a share and pays out forty percent, so the dividend is one dollar and twenty-eight cents. Its ex-date is a Wednesday, so Mateo must buy by Tuesday. Even a Wednesday purchase at the opening bell comes without the dividend. Then taxes. A qualified dividend comes from a domestic or qualified foreign corporation and must be held more than sixty days in the one hundred twenty-one day window that starts sixty days before the ex-date. It gets the zero, fifteen, or twenty percent rates. Fail either test and it's taxed at ordinary rates. A DRIP reinvests dividends into more shares with little or no commission. Here's the exam trap: reinvesting does not defer the tax. You're taxed in the year paid, but the reinvested amount raises your basis, so the same dollars aren't taxed again when you sell. With a client, you'd say: the DRIP is an automatic savings plan, you'll still see those dividends on your ten ninety-nine each year, and we track them so you don't pay tax on them twice.

equity.at: Stock dividends, splits and reverse splits
equity.say: Stock dividends, splits and reverse splits all do the same basic thing: they change the share count and the price per share, but not the company's value and not your ownership percentage. The company's assets and liabilities don't move, so it's a recapitalization, nothing more. Splits make shares affordable for small investors; reverse splits raise the price, often to avoid delisting. None of them is taxed when received, and your total basis stays the same, so the basis per share adjusts. Walk the example. Tallis is worth twenty-four million dollars with two million shares, so twelve dollars a share. It pays a twenty percent stock dividend. Two million times one point two is two point four million shares, and twenty-four million divided by two point four million is ten dollars. The wrong answer is cutting the price by the dividend percentage, which gives nine sixty. Separately, Priya owns two hundred Norland shares, cost forty-five, price ninety, before a three-for-two split. She ends up with three hundred shares at sixty dollars, still worth eighteen thousand. Her nine thousand dollar basis divided by three hundred shares is now thirty dollars a share. Common mistakes are treating three-for-two like two-for-one, or leaving basis per share unchanged. The exam trap: a stock dividend becomes taxable if the holder could have chosen cash instead, because of constructive receipt. With a client, you'd say: the split didn't make you richer, you have more shares at a lower price, same pie with smaller slices, and your cost per share drops too, which matters when you sell.

equity.at: Open-end funds: NAV, share classes and expenses
equity.say: Now investment companies, starting with the open-end mutual fund. It pools money for diversification and professional management under the objective in its prospectus. It sells and redeems its own shares, which don't trade on an exchange. The price is net asset value per share: total assets minus liabilities, divided by shares outstanding. It's priced at least once each business day, and forward pricing means your order gets the next NAV computed after you place it. Walk the example. Aldergrove holds forty-six point one million in securities and two point four million in cash, so forty-eight point five million in assets. Subtract one point three million of liabilities and you have forty-seven point two million. Divide by two point three six million shares and the NAV is exactly twenty dollars. Don't leave out the cash or the liabilities. Then share classes. A shares charge a front-end load at purchase and generally have the lowest total cost for long horizons. B shares charge a back-end load, a contingent deferred sales charge, on an early sale, which may be waived after about five years. C shares carry a level load, where the annual twelve b-one fee is the sales charge, every year. The expense ratio is annual operating expenses divided by average annual assets. The exam trap: a no-load fund may still charge twelve b-one fees, a hidden load, and a B share with a back-end charge is not no-load. With a client, you'd say: the price you get today is set after the market closes, so there's no point timing your order, and since you'll hold this twenty-plus years, the share class with the up-front charge usually ends up cheapest.

equity.at: Fund objectives: bond, equity, world, hybrid, metals, commodity
equity.say: Funds are grouped by broad objective, and for each one you want to know what it owns, what it's for, and its main risk. On the bond side, investment-grade funds hold bonds rated triple-B or higher. High-yield funds trade principal safety for high income. World bond funds carry currency risk and some of the highest bond fund expenses. And municipal funds pay interest free of federal tax. Now a key distinction: a bond fund has no maturity date, so if a client needs principal back on a specific date, a fund can't promise that. Walk the muni example. Nolan lives in Ohio and earns two thousand four hundred dollars from a national muni fund, with fifteen percent from Ohio issuers. Federally, it's all exempt. For Ohio, only the in-state share is exempt, three hundred sixty dollars, so two thousand forty is subject to Ohio tax. The mistake is assuming all muni interest is state-exempt. On the equity side, know the market cap ranges: small up to two billion, mid from two to ten billion, large over ten billion. Global means U.S. plus foreign; international means foreign only. Balanced funds run about sixty percent stock and forty percent bonds. Lifestyle funds hold a fixed risk level, while lifecycle, or target-date, funds get more conservative along a glide path. The exam trap: government bond funds have no credit risk but still lose value when rates rise. And correlation with U.S. stocks runs highest for developed markets, then emerging, then frontier. With a client, you'd say: since you're in a high bracket, a fund holding only our state's bonds keeps both federal and state tax off that income.

equity.at: Fund taxation and closed-end funds, UITs and SMAs
equity.say: Fund taxation first, because it surprises clients. Fund investors are taxed on what the fund distributes, whether or not they reinvest it, so they don't control the timing. Capital gain distributions are usually long-term no matter how long you've held the shares. Return of capital is nontaxable. And funds must pay out net realized gains by December thirty-first, which is why low-turnover funds can limit those distributions. Now the other pooled structures. A closed-end fund has a fixed number of shares after its I P O and trades on an exchange at a premium or discount to NAV. Because it has no redemptions to fund, the manager can hold less-liquid assets. A unit investment trust has fixed units and a limited life, and it's passive, chosen once and held. A separately managed account means the investor owns the securities directly, so you get your own cost basis per position and can exclude holdings, with minimums often fifty thousand dollars or more. Walk the UIT example. A bond trust starts with fifteen-year bonds. In year five rates fall, issuers call their bonds, and only twelve percent of the original principal is left. The prospectus allows termination below twenty-five percent, so the trust can liquidate and holders get their principal back years early. The exam trap: a closed-end investor can profit four ways, from distributed income, distributed gains, share price gains, and a narrowing discount or widening premium. With a client, you'd say: in a separately managed account you own each stock yourself, so we can keep out companies you don't want and pick which lots to sell for taxes.

equity.at: ETFs, hedge funds, funds of funds and GICs
equity.say: Four vehicles here. ETFs are mostly index-based funds that trade all day like stock. They track an index by replicating it, holding every security, or by sampling a representative subset. And in-kind redemption means an investor receives the underlying stock instead of cash, so it isn't taxed. Hedge funds are private, actively managed pools for wealthy, sophisticated investors. They're usually limited partnerships, with the manager as general partner and mostly accredited investors as limited partners, and the manager's pay is performance-based. The risks include leverage and little transparency. A fund of funds holds roughly ten to thirty hedge funds, adding diversification and opening access to nonaccredited investors, but it brings a second layer of fees and cash drag. GICs are insurer-guaranteed contracts, a bit like CDs, used mostly in retirement plans. A participating GIC has a variable rate that follows market rates, so you'd choose it when rates are expected to rise. A nonparticipating GIC is fixed, better when rates are expected to fall. Walk the example. Sofia wants cheap S and P five hundred exposure she can trade at noon, buy on margin and sell short. That points to an index ETF, not an index mutual fund. Pellham's four oh one k trustee expects rates to climb, so a participating GIC fits. The common mistakes are calling GICs risk-free and assuming ETFs are always passive. The exam trap: a GIC is not FDIC-insured, so it's slightly riskier than a CD despite the word guaranteed. With a client, you'd say: the stable-value option in your four oh one k is backed by an insurance company, not the FDIC, so its safety depends on that insurer.

Averaging techniques are formula plans for easing money into the market, and the way to keep them straight is to ask what stays fixed each period. Dollar cost averaging fixes the dollars, so a falling price buys more shares. Value averaging fixes a target rise in account value, so you invest even more when prices fall, and you can sell when you're above target. Share averaging fixes the share count, so you spend less when prices fall. Walk the dollar cost averaging example, because it hides a classic trap. Jun invests three thousand dollars a month at prices of twenty, fifteen, twenty-four and sixteen. He buys six hundred sixty-two and a half shares for twelve thousand dollars, so his average cost is about eighteen eleven. But the simple average price is eighteen seventy-five. Cost comes in lower because more shares were bought at the cheap prices. Don't report the average price as average cost. And notice, at sixteen dollars his shares are worth ten thousand six hundred, a fourteen hundred dollar loss. DCA lowers cost; it doesn't guarantee a profit. For value averaging with a two thousand dollar monthly target, you invest the target minus what the account is already worth, so total investment of five thousand four hundred over two hundred forty shares gives a twenty-two fifty average cost. The exam trap: DCA works best in falling or choppy markets and worst in a steady rise, where a lump sum up front buys more. With a client, you'd say: putting in the same amount every month means you automatically buy more when prices are on sale.

equity.at: Cost basis methods for fund shares
equity.say: Cost basis decides how much gain you report. Gain or loss is net sale proceeds minus adjusted basis, and basis means the purchase price plus commissions plus reinvested dividends and distributions. When you bought shares at different times and prices, the method decides which cost gets matched to the shares you sell. Specific identification names the exact lots, needs good records, and in a rising market is the most favorable, because you pick the high-cost lots. Average cost gives every share the same basis and is the most commonly used. FIFO, first in first out, is the IRS default, and in a rising market it's the least favorable, because the oldest shares are the cheapest. Walk Dmitri's example. He owns two hundred shares at ten, three hundred at fourteen, and two hundred fifty at eighteen, seven hundred fifty shares costing ten thousand seven hundred. He sells two hundred at twenty, for four thousand dollars. Under FIFO, basis is two thousand, so the gain is two thousand. Under average cost, each share is about fourteen twenty-seven, so the gain is about eleven hundred forty-seven. Under specific ID, choosing the eighteen dollar lot, the gain is only four hundred. The common mistake is averaging the three lot prices instead of weighting by shares. The exam trap: reinvested exempt-interest dividends from a muni fund also raise basis, even though they were never taxed, and selling muni fund shares is still a taxable event. With a client, you'd say: every reinvested dividend counts as part of what you paid, and if we pick which shares to sell instead of letting the oldest go first, we can shrink the taxable gain.

equity.at: Fund selection: objective, holdings, flexibility and risk
equity.say: Fund selection starts with the client, not the fund. Rank the client's objectives, whether income, appreciation, or preservation, because one fund can't do all three at once. Then match the fund's objective and risk to them, and confirm what the fund actually owns and how much freedom its manager has. Remember the portfolio view: total portfolio risk matters more than one fund's risk, so a volatile fund with low correlation can still fit a cautious client. Then check the actual holdings in the annual, semiannual and quarterly reports. Forty percent or more in one sector reads aggressive; no industry above fifteen percent reads more conservative. Walk Ava's example, because it shows why the label isn't enough. She puts thirty percent of her portfolio in what she thinks is an all-stock fund, but the manager is really seventy-five percent stocks and twenty-five percent cash. Thirty percent times seventy-five percent means only twenty-two and a half percent of her portfolio is in stock through that fund, and seven and a half percent is cash. Her plan is more conservative than intended. The mistakes are trusting the fund's name and judging aggressiveness from what the prospectus allows rather than what the fund holds. The exam trap: the fund's objective must match both the client's objective and their risk tolerance; one alone isn't enough. With a client, you'd say: your stock fund is holding a quarter of its money in cash, so let's use funds that stay fully invested and keep your mix where we set it.

equity.at: Performance, fees, turnover, taxes and pitfalls
equity.say: Last section, judging performance. Past returns don't reliably predict future returns, but consistency, costs and tax drag are measurable and they persist. So judge funds over full cycles, against true peers, and after adjusting for risk. Walk the example. Ten thousand dollars goes into Fund X, which gains twenty percent then loses ten, and Fund Y, which gains forty then loses twenty-five. You compound, you don't add. X ends at ten thousand eight hundred; Y ends at ten thousand five hundred. Steadiness wins, and here's why: a loss needs a bigger gain to recover. A forty percent drop needs about sixty-seven percent just to break even. Now costs. Fund X's expense ratio is its management, twelve b-one and other expenses added up, zero point nine five percent, and the front load is excluded. Turnover uses the lesser of purchases or sales over average assets, so ninety million over three hundred million is thirty percent. The mistakes are putting loads or commissions in the expense ratio and using the larger figure for turnover. Look for five and ten year records covering a bull and a bear cycle. High turnover brings trading costs that sit outside the expense ratio, plus more realized gains. Watch for survivorship bias and buying the distribution right before a big year-end payout. The exam trap: growth funds can throw off large taxable distributions in bull years even if you never sell, and tax-inefficient funds belong in tax-deferred accounts. With a client, you'd say: this fund looks great on a one-year chart, but it fell much harder than its peers last downturn, and the steadier, cheaper fund has actually left investors with more money.
